Breaking.title: Huntingdon train knifeman guilty of trying to murder 14 people
Breaking.text:
A knifeman has been found guilty of attempting to murder 14 people, including 10 on board a train to London.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Anthony Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Some hid in toilets and bike racks before the driver was forced to make an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, where Williams was arrested by armed police.

As well as the train attacks, Williams, of Langford Road, Peterborough, was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Jurors deliberated for 15 hours and 53 minutes before delivering seven guilty verdicts, and then returned an hour later to give the final seven.

The judge, Mr Justice Calver KC, said the victims handled themselves with "great dignity throughout" the trial.

Aside from the attack on the LNER train, Williams also attempted to murder a boy and two men in Peterborough on 31 October 2025, and then a teenager on a DLR train in east London hours later.

The defendant, who appeared at court via a video link from a secure hospital, showed little emotion as each verdict was delivered.

Reacting to the verdicts, Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The fact that nobody was killed in his rampage is down to the courage, quick thinking and good fortune of the people he attacked."

It has now emerged that in the month before the attacks, Williams twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

A spokesperson for NHS East of England said it would be investigating the care provided to Williams.

Cambridgeshire Police has also apologised for missed opportunities "that may have prevented" the stabbings.

Assistant Chief Constable Leighton Hammett said an alleged assault in Peterborough on 27 September 2025, several weeks before the train attacks, had been linked to Williams.

Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said two officers faced misconduct proceedings over their handling of the incident and the investigation remained ongoing.

Williams's knife attack on the LNER service began when he stabbed Jonathan Gjoshe – then a Scunthorpe United footballer – at 19:37 GMT.

The defender later informed police his whole arm was "drenched with blood".

Other victims included Scott Bletcher, stabbed six times in his seat as he returned from a Christmas shopping trip.

Bletcher told jurors he thought, "This is what it feels like to die" after being knifed.

The court also heard from Nottingham Forest football fan Stephen Crean, who decided "he had to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

CCTV footage played to the jury showed LNER staff member Samir Zitouni use a frying pan to fend off Williams.

He said to the knifeman "we love you, we can help you" as he thought it was "better than swearing at him".

After the train stopped, Zitouni fell between the train and the platform. His lungs were punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.

Having been arrested in Huntingdon railway station's car park, Williams was said to be "acting strangely" and "completely unfazed by what had occurred... he was rocking and laughing".

If you've been a victim of crime, details of help and support are available at BBC Action Line.

One police officer noted he "appeared to be talking to himself" and spoke about the devil.

Consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Bernard Chin told the trial Williams, who did not give evidence in his defence, was "suffering from an acute relapse of schizophrenia" at the time of the attacks.

Jurors heard Williams had "the delusional premise that his life was at risk by a wide-ranging conspiracy by the devil".

A passenger texted British Transport Police (BTP) reporting a male behaving erratically, but the man dropped down on to the tracks at Stevenage and police officers deemed it unsafe to pursue him.

Then, in the early hours of 1 November, Williams sliced the face of teenager Isaiah Idris on a DLR train in east London with a knife.

Idris described how his attacker had repeatedly asked: "Are you beefing the devil?"

Det Supt Sam Blackburn, from BTP, said Williams' offending had sparked "one of the most significant and complex" investigations in the force's history.

"The events that unfolded onboard the train on 1 November were unlike anything previously encountered before, and Anthony Williams created what I can only describe as a terrifying scene of fear and violence."

Breaking.title: Huntingdon knifeman told doctor psychosis drugs weren't working
Breaking.text:
Hurtling along at more than 120mph, passengers on an East Coast Mainline train bound for London King's Cross found themselves caught up in one of the worst acts of violence on Britain's rail network in recent times.

Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people in five minutes on board the train last November, near Huntingdon, in Cambridgeshire, leaving some seriously injured. On Thursday, a jury found him guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.

It has now emerged that, in the month before that attack, the knifeman had twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

But he never saw a doctor and did not receive additional mental health treatment.

Now his trial at Cambridge Crown Court is over, BBC News can also report his long history of violent criminality, revealed through old court transcripts we have obtained.

It stretched back two decades. In his teens Williams robbed people at knife point, including on a train. Even after he had started his 25-hour rampage, culminating in the Huntingdon attack, there were potential opportunities to arrest him.

Williams, who was born Anthony Abiola Oluwatuyi in London in 1993, first arrived on the police radar aged 12, when he was excluded from school for arson after setting fire to the toilets.

One acquaintance from the time - who would only speak on condition of anonymity - told BBC News Williams would "turn people's pockets inside out just because he wanted to". They said: "He was a thug who brought a knife to class."

Over the next seven years, he was convicted of 14 further offences, including five thefts, three robberies, and two offences of possession of a knife.

In October 2012, aged 19, he robbed two fellow teenagers of their smartphones at knife point on a train, warning them: "If you tell, I will come back and find you."

By the time Williams appeared at St Albans Crown Court in February 2020 he was a crack cocaine and heroin addict, as well as a drug dealer.

He had been arrested the previous year in possession of heroin, crack cocaine and cannabis, as well as a pair of scales and 12 "burner" phones. Asked about his drug dealing, he told police: "If I don't do it, not good things will happen to me."

He was sentenced to four years in prison, where he was sectioned and held in a psychiatric hospital until his release.

Upon release, he moved to Peterborough to live with his mother and stepfather. At this stage it is unclear exactly what mental health treatment he received there, but the BBC understands that, following last year's train attack, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust launched an internal review.

On 30 September 2025 - a month before the Huntingdon attack - Williams contacted his GP online about what he described as his "deteriorating mental state", saying his drugs were not working.

The doctor told him he should be taking 200mg of the Quetiapine he had been prescribed to treat his paranoid schizophrenia, but he was only taking 100mg.

The GP invited him to a meeting on 14 October which he did not attend. Williams contacted the doctor again on 23 October, again saying the medication was ineffective - but he did not respond when the GP tried to get back to him.

In a phone call with a taxi firm on 31 October, the night before the train attack, Williams can be heard apparently speaking to voices in his head, saying things like "devil wanna play", and making strange noises, before then resuming the conversation normally.

Following the attack, Williams told psychiatrists "things were bad" in the days before it.

"I was paranoid people were going to attack me. They were coming for me. I was hearing a lot of voices, feeling a lot of fear," he said. "I just needed to protect myself. It was me or them."

Psychiatrists who assessed Williams after the attack concluded he had been "acutely psychotic".

Dr Bernard Chin said Williams was suffering from "paranoid persecutory delusions" that he was the focus of "an organised conspiracy that came about because of the machinations of the devil".

Following the guilty verdicts, NHS England's East of England division said it would commission an independent investigation into the healthcare provided to Williams "to help identify any opportunities for learning and improvement".

On the morning of the Huntingdon attack, on 1 November, Williams stabbed a teenager on a Docklands Light Railway (DLR) train near Pontoon Dock station, in east London. British Transport Police (BTP) said initial CCTV of the attack was of poor quality.

However, the force tracked the knifeman to nearby Poplar DLR station where officers obtained clearer CCTV images.

Using reactive facial recognition software they generated a match with Williams, who had two addresses recorded on police systems - one in Waltham Cross, in Hertfordshire, the other in Peterborough.

Officers prioritised the Waltham Cross address because there was a "recent financial trace" to it, and it was closer to the DLR attack.

At 6:48pm that day, BTP officers turned up at the address to arrest Williams. But half an hour earlier, at 6:16pm, Williams had left his actual home - in Peterborough - to travel to the station and launch his stabbing spree on a London North Eastern Railway (LNER) train.

BTP Deputy Chief Constable Stuart Cundy said "it was certainly not for want of trying by the officers who responded and commenced our investigation immediately after the attack on the train at Pontoon Dock".

But when it comes to other incidents during Williams' chequered past, whether criminal or health-related, various authorities will now have to assess whether anything could have been done before he boarded that LNER train.

Additional reporting by Robbie Kalus

Breaking.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
Breaking.text:
Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.

Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.

The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

Breaking.title: Drug rape husband says wife 'would have been terrified', court hears
Breaking.text:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A husband who admits drugging and raping his wife with strangers has told a court that if she had woken during the abuse, she would have been "terrified".

The defendant, who has admitted multiple sexual offences dating back to 2004, said he drugged his wife so she would be unaware of the abuse by him and other men.

He changed his pleas earlier this year and admitted offences including rape, sexual assault and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence, as well as inviting 13 other men to take part in the abuse.

Nine of those men have pleaded not guilty to sexual offences against the woman and are standing trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, entered the witness box to give evidence for the prosecution.

The court has heard that the man, who is in his 60s, filmed and photographed his offending as his wife lay "out of it" on their bed before sharing the material online.

Prosecutors say that, by 2023 at the latest, he had begun inviting other men to the couple's home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, where it is alleged they sexually abused her while she was unconscious.

Asked by prosecutor Louise Oakley KC why he was now telling the truth, he said: "So the court knows what happened. So my wife knows and my children know.

"I am here to tell the truth and give my account of what actually happened."

He told jurors he had drugged his wife so she would be unaware of the abuse by him and other men.

"She would never agree to do any of this," he said. "She would have been terrified and scream."

Following his guilty pleas in September, the husband gave police a written statement detailing his offending.

He told the jury the process had been "very difficult" because of the "guilt and shame" he felt and the "pain" he had caused his wife.

He accepted responsibility for his actions and for facilitating contact between other men and his wife.

Asked whether she had ever consented to what happened to her, he replied: "Never."

He said his wife did not know any of the men he invited to the house and had never spoken to them.

Breaking.title: Andy Burnham joined by former PMs for Widdecombe service
Breaking.text:
Andy Burnham was joined by former prime ministers as he attended a memorial service for the late politician Ann Widdecombe.

Hundreds gathered for the Service of Remembrance at Westminster Cathedral on Thursday afternoon, including David Cameron, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and deputy leader Richard Tice, along with former Conservative Chancellor Philip Hammond and Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle, were also in attendance.

Bishop James Curry, the Auxiliary Bishop of Westminster, led the service after the Archbishop of Westminster, Richard Moth, was taken to hospital earlier.

Moth, who is the head of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, underwent tests after he "felt unwell", Westminster Diocese said.

During the memorial, tributes were paid by Widdecombe's nephew, Reverend Roger Widdecombe, and independent crossbencher Lord Alton of Liverpool.

Widdecombe's nephew said his aunt's death was "a tragedy," but added the service was to "pay tribute to Aunt Ann" and "celebrate and thank God for a life well lived".

He said: "Words such as integrity, brave, kind, delightful, indefatigable, interested, tireless, fun, all express something of the amazing woman that Ann was."

He noted his aunt was "certainly a lot of fun," recalling family anecdotes which prompted guests to laugh.

Finishing the eulogy, he said: "We loved her very much, and we'll miss her."

She became a member of Reform in 2019 as a party spokeswoman.

Away from politics, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

Breaking.title: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field
Breaking.text:
Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.

The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.

The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.

Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.

But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.

The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills.

"The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder.

"What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."

It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.

The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.

Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.

But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.

Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.

They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge.

A number of MPs say they have heard conflicting claims - with both outcomes being predicted.

What is clearer is that the government's decision will be controversial, whichever way it goes. There is a private and public battle playing out.

Backers of the scheme argue approving it would provide an economic boost. The Conservatives also say it would enhance energy security.

But oil is traded internationally – and the energy secretary has said approving the scheme will not help with immediate cost of living pressures. Rosebank would also be more polluting than Jackdaw, a gas field, which was approved last month.

A fortnight ago, backers of the field were confident it would be approved.

They believed the chancellor's language on energy bills at the Budget, coupled with the lack of political jeopardy that materialised from the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, had made their case stronger.

The same group of MPs believe it would be difficult to reject Rosebank around the same time the prime minister is set to deliver a 10-year plan focused on reindustrialisation.

The government has said oil and gas would be part of the energy mix for many years to come and sources in the trade union movement have suggested that if Rosebank doesn't go ahead, existing inward investment in the North Sea would be put at risk.

While Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields", it does pledge to honour existing ones.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

The mood among some pro-Rosebank MPs changed this week, with several who back approval telling the BBC they were now worried it would be blocked.

The BBC has spoken privately to Labour MPs involved in the debate, before the letter was sent to the prime minister, to get a sense of how divisive it is proving.

One ministerial aide said: "There are quite a few of us who are considering our positions. I'm in that group. We want to see leadership on climate change."

Another aide who said they might quit added: "There a group of us for whom we became Labour MPs because of climate change. It is the issue that motivated us into politics."

Other aides – known in Westminster as parliamentary private secretaries – told the BBC they were opposed, but would stay in their jobs if it went ahead.

Another said they thought there were increasing signs the prime minister would not be able to carry his party with him if the scheme was given the thumbs up.

And another said the energy secretary might have to resign if it goes ahead, given her scepticism about the project.

It has been reported in recent weeks that members of her team are encouraging opponents to make their feelings known. The BBC has been told the same.

One MP, who backs Rosebank, said the behind-the-scenes operation had been so effective, the scheme was up in the air again.

That has led to some anger at the energy secretary.

One minister says: "Miatta has boxed herself in with how she's handled Rosebank. It's outrageous if she's encouraging MPs to speak up over Rosebank. We should get on and do it."

Like the decision itself, the exact timeframe is unclear. But some opposition figures expect it mid-December.

Whatever happens, it will be controversial and has already exposed splits in the Labour Party.

Breaking.title: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction
Breaking.text:
Disgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.

Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.

A government minister, Anna Turley, told LBC, external she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, and that "for too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass".

Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.

During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"

Asked again, he replies: "I'd lost the plot."

The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."

Despite that apparent combative stance, Edwards wrote on his blog on Thursday: "I want viewers to know that I did not avoid a single question, and that I answered each as honestly as I could, including those about deeply personal matters: my relationships, my temperament, my sexuality."

Explaining his reasons for giving the interviews, he said: "My difficulties became front-page news, and the account that took hold was, in places, misleading or simply untrue.

"Those promoting false narratives are also, unsurprisingly, the ones questioning my right to set the record straight.

"I was left with a choice: to let that faulty account stand forever, or to offer my own."

In a statement, Forbes said it was "an important film to make".

"It's rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues – whether it's celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment," he said.

Channel 4's documentary, titled Huw Edwards - Guilty, will be broadcast on Tuesday.

In the clip for his separate interview with the Observer and its Tortoise Investigates podcast, Edwards is seen saying: "Lots of the advice I've had is just be quiet, don't say anything."

Interviewer Ceri Thomas, a former editor of the BBC's Today programme and Panorama, said he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

The interviews have been criticised by two people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday that Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Meanwhile Rosamund Urwin, chief news correspondent for the Sunday Times, who jointly led the paper's 2023 investigation into Russell Brand, reacted to Thomas's statement by saying: "An 'unbelievable terrible fix' is quite the euphemism for someone viewing child abuse images of victims as young as 7."

The podcast will be released on Tuesday. Tortoise Media, which owns the Observer, has a deal to make some podcasts available on BBC Sounds, but the BBC said the Huw Edwards series would not be among them.

Channel 4 and the Observer said Edwards had received no payment for the interviews or had any editorial input.

Breaking.title: Mandelson kept lobby firm shares for months as US ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
Breaking.text:
Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026, the same month the company went into administration.

Emails about his dealings with his Washington counterparts show a close relationship, with one message from an unnamed White House official in April 2025 telling Lord Mandelson his label as the "Prince of Darkness" could not be "farther from the truth".

Ahead of a speech he was due to give on Britain's role "in the age of Trump", documents show him seeking advice from a Global Counsel employee in August 2025, during his time as ambassador.

The exchange contains feedback from an unnamed Global Counsel director, who suggested he should use "warmer language" about China and tone down "parts of your apologia of the Trump administration".

The director warned: "Scepticism of [the Trump administration] is now so deep – at least in the public policy-interested world outside government – that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid."

Lord Mandelson responds to say he would water down his language, and in another email tries to arrange an "under the radar" lunch meeting to discuss China and trade between a GC employee and someone from the US President's Council of Economic Advisers.

On the domestic front, Lord Mandelson also sent texts to Sir Keir's then chief of staff Morgan McSweeney in September 2025 offering advice on a cabinet reshuffle.

He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to "solve your Darren issue", although McSweeney did not respond until after the reshuffle decisions had been made, with Jones given a newly-created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.

Lord Mandelson has yet to comment on the most recent release of papers relating to his appointment.

He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

No charges have been made. A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street garden following the release of the documents, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address culture change for Westminster as part of his 10 year plan, which he said will be published next month.

He said: "I've come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country and to strengthen the public interests when it comes to all of these issues."

Security minister Dan Jarvis told MPs: "The government recognises that action needs to be taken in response to the issues raised by Mandelson's appointment."

He said action had already been taken to strengthen the vetting and appointments process, including strengthening the management of conflicts of interest.

Future appointments will not be made before security clearance has been granted, he said, adding that review by Sir Adrian Fulford of vetting procedures was nearing completion.

A separate review by Sir Anthony Finkelstein into use of personal messaging services including WhatsApp and Signal for business purposes is expected to be published in January next year.

Breaking.title: Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua: Boxing chiefs to assess fighter's mental health
Breaking.text:
The British Boxing Board of Control is looking into Tyson Fury's comments about his schizophrenia diagnosis but is "fairly confident" the British heavyweight will be cleared to fight Anthony Joshua next month.

Fury, 38, is due to face Joshua at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, with the ringwalk expected in the early hours of 12 December.

In a Netflix documentary out on Friday, he says he heard voices threatening him and his family in the months after he beat Wladimir Klitschko to become world champion in 2015.

"We are in the process of dealing with the matter but if there are any medical issues we wouldn't let anyone box, doesn't matter if it's Tyson Fury or not, it could be anybody," Robert Smith, the board's general secretary, told BBC Sport.

"I'm fairly confident he will be absolutely fine. We're dealing with it now and we'll have an answer very shortly."

Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, external, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion it sees fit".

Smith would not say what the process would involve over the next few days, saying "it's a medical matter".

He said that all boxers on the card will undergo medical checks, adding: "If our doctors are satisfied he's fit to box, he will box."

In the documentary, Fury and his wife Paris recall his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.

Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.

The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.

The heavyweight, who struggled with drug and alcohol addiction after beating Klitschko, says a Halloween night out in 2017 prompted him to return to training, calling that a "turning point" after being "embarrassed by how I looked".

He went on to beat Deontay Wilder in 2020 to become world heavyweight champion for a second time.

Breaking.title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
Breaking.text:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

Breaking.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
Breaking.text:
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

Breaking.title: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
Breaking.text:
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.

The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.

The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.

"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.

Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.

That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.

The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

Business.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
Business.text:
More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.

That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.

On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

Business.title: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
Business.text:
The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing.

The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.

They point to improving sales over recent months as proof the business had a future.

MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".

Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised.

First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year.

The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme.

Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates.

In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it.

Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth.

It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely.

Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup."

Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff.

But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed.

Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them.

In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees.

Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers.

But if, as some retail veterans have told the BBC, Gordon Brothers never really intended to turn this business around, why would the previous owners PepCo give them a no-lose gamble? Why didn't they do what Gordon Brothers are doing - profiting with no risk?

The answer is simple: Pepco have other businesses, which could have got tangled up in the administration of Poundland.

Business.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
Business.text:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

That depends on who you ask.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

That depends on what happens next.

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

Business.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
Business.text:
Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments.

Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton.

The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments.

The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria.

The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954.

In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars.

Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.

Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music.

These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute.

When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers.

The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design.

But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in Düsseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection, external of the Stratocaster design in Germany.

The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The Düsseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections.

The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author".

It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms".

On its website, Fender announced in March, external the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced".

Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe.

One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products".

The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars.

The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians.

"Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments.

Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole.

"We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action."

The letter, he says, came as a shock.

"For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions."

In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier.

"As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action."

Thomann says he was taking legal action not just for his company, but for smaller music companies too.

"We used to be a small music shop ourselves," he says.

"Many of the smaller manufacturers, guitar makers and dealers affected simply don't have the financial and legal resources to conduct a legal dispute like this."

One such company is LSL Instruments, a family-owned boutique guitar maker in California. Its director of sales, Johny Miller, told me that when they first received Fender's letter they were "pretty terrified and blown away".

"They were asking us to retrieve guitars from dealers out there and destroy them and send them proof.

"So when we heard Hans Thomann got the same letter and responded by suing them… so that everybody in the guitar community could understand exactly what's going on… we were so thankful and grateful," he says.

Fender tells BBC that it agrees that "legal clarity was important", and that it was now focusing more on targeting larger manufacturers.

It also says it realises that "our outreach has caused concern and frustration, particularly among smaller, independent guitar builders. "To them we say: we continue to hear you, and we're listening."

Business.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
Business.text:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.

The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.

The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.

Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.

One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.

The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.

PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.

In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.

"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".

He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.

Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.

"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.

"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."

Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."

Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.

Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.

It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.

But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.

Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.

This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.

In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.

In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.

After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".

However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.

Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.

If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

Business.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
Business.text:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year, set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

Business.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
Business.text:
The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

Business.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
Business.text:
Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements could face further delays to compensation after the financial regulator said it had made some errors in its calculations.

Driver have already been told they must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement.

Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed.

The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.

Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.

The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.

The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much.

Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.

Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders.

Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything.

The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company.

The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts.

Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation.

The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain, external.

lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge

those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster

some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026

some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014

there are exemptions, external, and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation

those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed

those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim

Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees.

FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers.

Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027.

But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme.

The watchdog has now said it uncovered some mistakes in how it categorised a small group of loan agreements under its redress scheme, which could have a small impact on compensation levels.

"While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects the ongoing litigation," the FCA said. That could leave average payouts somewhere between £819 and £839.

"We will discuss with the challengers and the court the impact on this deadline, and for the timeline of the litigation."

Consumer Voice has said the scheme leaves "too many people short-changed". The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance.

The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.

It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes.

The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme. Without a scheme in place, the FCA has estimated that up to 19 million complaints would need to be handled individually, taking three years and costing lenders £6bn more.

It said it would "defend the scheme robustly as lawful and the best way to resolve such a widespread, long running and complex issue".

Ultimately, the industry is expected to cover the full costs of any compensation scheme, including any administrative costs.

Lenders - including some of the UK's biggest banks and specialist motor finance firms - have already set aside billions of pounds for potential payouts.

The body that represents the lending industry, the Finance and Leasing Association, said it had "concerns" about the central programme but that it was choosing not to raise a legal challenge.

Santander, Barclays and Lloyds also accepted the scheme, despite raising concerns that the level of redress is disproportionate to those who suffered harm.

Even if drivers are entitled to compensation from these lenders they will need to wait.

There were some concessions made to lenders in a scaled-down final compensation plan from the FCA.

The Supreme Court considered three test cases which influenced the FCA's decision and, ultimately, limited how broad the compensation programme could have been.

It focused on whether the car dealers had a duty to act on behalf of their customers, rather than in their own interests. The test case which was upheld was that of Marcus Johnson, who bought his first car - a Suzuki Swift - in 2017.

In his case, the Supreme Court said the terms of his finance deal were unfair due of the size of the commission payment, and the fact he appeared to have been misled over the relationship between the finance firm and the dealer.
